title: The Chemist Who Invented Synthetic Indigo
event_summary: In 1897, the German chemical company BASF began mass-producing synthetic indigo developed by chemist Adolf von Baeyer's decades-long research, offering a cheap, consistent alternative to the natural dye. Within a single decade, India's indigo plantations—which had supplied nearly the entire world's blue dye for centuries and employed millions—collapsed almost completely. The multi-billion-dollar crop that had shaped colonial economies, fueled the slave trade, and provoked violent uprisings like the 1859 Indigo Revolt was rendered economically irrelevant by a laboratory process.
why_forgotten: The story falls awkwardly between disciplines: too chemical for colonial historians, too colonial for chemists. European narratives celebrated synthetic indigo as a triumph of industrial chemistry without examining the devastation it wrought on South Asian farming communities. Indian historiography focused on political independence movements rather than the quiet economic annihilation of an entire agricultural sector.
why_it_matters: The synthetic indigo revolution was the first time a laboratory product completely destroyed a global agricultural commodity, establishing the template by which petrochemical industries would later replace natural rubber, silk, and fertilizers. It accelerated the impoverishment of Bengal's rural population, deepening the economic preconditions for the devastating 1943 Bengal Famine. Today, every pair of blue jeans in the world descends from this moment—and the current push to develop bio-indigo reflects a belated reckoning with the environmental toxicity of synthetic dye production.
